books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Slaughter-House Cases, 83 U.S. 36 (1873), majority opinion of Justice Samuel F. Miller

stimulus.text:
“It is quite clear, then, that there is a citizenship of the United States, and a citizenship of a State, which are distinct from each other, and which depend upon different characteristics or circumstances in the individual. . . . it is only the former which are placed by this clause under the protection of the Federal Constitution, and that the latter, whatever they may be, are not intended to have any additional protection by this paragraph of the amendment.”

—Justice Samuel F. Miller, majority opinion, Slaughter-House Cases, 1873
stimulus.source_note: Slaughter-House Cases, 83 U.S. 36 (1873), majority opinion of Justice Samuel F. Miller. Public domain (U.S. Supreme Court opinion; text verified against the National Constitution Center excerpt and Cornell LII). Ellipses mark omissions inside the passage.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The butchers who brought the case argued that Louisiana’s slaughterhouse monopoly violated their rights. The Court’s answer mattered for Reconstruction mainly because

options.text: it upheld the Louisiana legislature’s power to regulate business.
options.misconception: The business ruling is the case’s surface; its lasting effect was the narrow reading of the Fourteenth Amendment.

options.text: it narrowed the Fourteenth Amendment for later civil rights cases.
it struck down the Fourteenth Amendment as unconstitutional.
options.misconception: The Court upheld the amendment; it narrowed what the amendment protected.

options.text: it ordered Louisiana to end its Reconstruction government.
options.misconception: Background: the Court did no such thing; Louisiana’s Reconstruction government fell later, by politics.

rationales.A: The business ruling is the case’s surface; its lasting effect was the narrow reading of the Fourteenth Amendment.
rationales.B: The case was about butchers, but Miller’s reasoning about citizenship became the tool later courts used to turn away civil rights claims. A business dispute ended up shrinking the amendment meant to protect freedpeople.
rationales.C: The Court upheld the amendment; it narrowed what the amendment protected.
rationales.D: Background: the Court did no such thing; Louisiana’s Reconstruction government fell later, by politics.
rationales.general:
1. The butchers were white tradesmen fighting a monopoly, not freedpeople fighting for rights.
2. But Miller answered them by defining the Fourteenth Amendment’s reach.
3. His narrow definition became the rule later courts quoted when civil rights claims came before them.
4. So a case about meat markets ended up shrinking the amendment that guarded freedom.
Remember: the most important part of a case is often not the dispute that started it.
